source.title: Challenges and open problems in computational prediction of protein complexes: the case of membrane complexes

accepted.question_text: How can computational methods extract the membrane protein subinteractome, meaning the set of interactions among membrane proteins, so that membrane protein complexes can be reconstructed from membrane-protein interaction data despite the scarcity of characterized membrane complexes with known protein-protein interactions?

evidence.quote: One major avenue is to understand membrane proteins and their complexes is to map the membrane protein ‘subinteractomes’, the set of interactions among membrane proteins.
The need now is to develop effective computational techniques to mine this membrane subinteractome data to reconstruct membrane complexes.
a) How to extract out the membrane ‘subinteractome’? • Very few membrane complexes characterised for PPIs.

accepted.question_text: How should interactions in a membrane protein subinteractome, the set of interactions among membrane proteins, be filtered when the resulting network is already sparse, and should that filtering use only the membrane subnetwork or also information from the whole protein interaction network or neighboring soluble proteins?

evidence.quote: One major avenue is to understand membrane proteins and their complexes is to map the membrane protein ‘subinteractomes’, the set of interactions among membrane proteins.
b) How to filter these interactions (since the network will already be sparse)? • Combine it with the whole network or neighbors among soluble proteins for this process?

accepted.question_text: When a computational method clusters a membrane protein interaction network, do the resulting clusters correspond to real membrane protein complexes, understood as groups formed by physical interactions among membrane proteins, especially when many observed interactions are transient?
accepted.context_brief: validity of clusters as membrane complexes

evidence.quote: Among these, membrane protein complexes are formed by physical interaction among membrane proteins.
c) Do clusters correspond to membrane complexes? • Obstacle: Too many transient interactions.

accepted.question_text: Given dynamic exchange, meaning transient exchange of proteins into and out of existing membrane complexes, should computational prediction methods detect multiple alternative forms of the same membrane protein complex rather than a single fixed complex?
accepted.context_brief: detecting alternative forms of dynamic complexes

evidence.quote: Many membrane complexes are formed by transient interactions involving exchange of proteins in and out of existing complexes – a phenomenon called ‘dynamic exchange’.
There is dynamic exchange of proteins happens across complexes. So, different “isophorms” of the same complex should be detected?

accepted.question_text: Where can time information about membrane-complex assembly or dynamic exchange be obtained, and how can that time information, together with chaperone information when available, be incorporated into clustering or other computational methods for identifying and analyzing membrane complexes?
accepted.context_brief: using time and chaperone information in clustering

evidence.quote: This will involve identification of membrane complexes from the yeast membrane subinteractome, followed by incorporation of chaperone and, if available, ‘time’ information to study the assembly of membrane complexes.
Where to obtain “time” information for this and how to incorporate into the clustering?

accepted.question_text: How should predicted membrane protein complexes be evaluated when very few bona fide, known membrane complexes are available as validation benchmarks, while predicted putative complexes may themselves need experimental validation and may help assign roles to unannotated proteins?
accepted.context_brief: evaluation with few known membrane complexes

evidence.quote: d) How to evaluate the complexes, since very few bona fide complexes are known?
All the more interesting because we can provide putative complexes for validation! • We can also assign roles to unannotated proteins.

accepted.question_text: How can computational analyses study complex-formation relationships between membrane proteins and soluble proteins?

evidence.quote: e) Studying the relationships (complex formations) between membrane proteins and soluble proteins.

accepted.question_text: What explains why membrane complexes assemble in an ordered manner through intermediaries aided by chaperones, given that the purpose of this ordering is unclear and has only been suggested to protect cells against harmful intermediaries?

evidence.quote: Studies reveal that this assembly occurs in an orderly fashion, that is, membrane complexes are formed by an ordered assembly of intermediaries, and in order to prevent unwanted intermediaries, this assembly is highly aided by chaperones.
Why membrane complexes assemble in an ordered manner is unclear, but studies suggest that this could be a protection mechanism of the cell against harmful intermediaries.

trace.notes: Normalized the arXiv abs URL to https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.01863.pdf and downloaded the exact PDF source to the parser temporary directory.

Mapped the PDF title, sections, terminology, and likely open-question regions. The paper contains Background on pages 1-3, Challenges on pages 3-4, Open computational problems on pages 4-5, and References on pages 5-7.
Extracted an implicit unresolved question from the Challenges section because the source explicitly states that the reason for ordered membrane-complex assembly is unclear.

Extracted the explicit open computational problems listed in Section 3, including subquestions about filtering, clustering, dynamic exchange, time information, evaluation, and membrane-soluble protein relationships.
Expanded membrane subinteractome using the source definition and tied the question to reconstruction of membrane complexes from interaction data.
Restated the filtering problem with the source's sparse-network constraint and its proposed comparison between whole-network and soluble-neighbor information.
Expanded the cluster-validity question with the source's definition of membrane protein complexes and the stated obstacle of transient interactions.
Expanded the alternative-form detection question using the source definition of dynamic exchange.
Merged the time-information subquestion with the prior requirement to incorporate chaperone and time information when studying membrane-complex assembly.
Expanded evaluation of complexes by including the source's scarcity of known bona fide complexes and downstream validation/annotation motivations.
Restated the source's final open problem as a standalone computational-analysis question about membrane-soluble protein complex formation relationships.
Rewrote the source's unclear ordered-assembly statement as a self-contained question grounded in the stated role of intermediaries and chaperones.

Merged the general computational-methods-for-assembly candidate into the more specific time/chaperone-information question and kept the ordered-assembly explanation question distinct because it asks why the assembly ordering occurs.

All accepted questions have source-text evidence with numeric PDF pages, no source-pointing language in question_text, no unresolved cross-references, and meta.is_solved=false because the source does not mark any item solved.
